Internal — NARA archive crawler / OpenSearch ingestion

Deletion Decision Tree

For the Weikai deletion-safety conversation (Sep 2–21, 2026) — updated fork, Sep 22, 2026

Corrected fork
The original version of this document (RkPrgNN5s1…) described the tombstone design as internally floated and never adopted, and closed Weikai's "just don't delete on a failed fetch" request as unreconcilable with contracted scope. Neither is true anymore. Tombstoning shipped — archive_crawler and nara-opensearch-lambda, both on a tombstone branch, committed and pushed — and it resolves the core conflict section 02 below describes, using data the crawler already computed and was discarding, not a new re-verification pipeline. Sections 03, 04, and 06 are rewritten against the shipped logic. Sections 01, 02, and 05 keep their original shape, corrected where the old conclusion no longer holds.
01

Where this comes from

Weikai raised the same concern twice — once about a full purge risking empty search results, once about the timestamp-based reconciliation that replaced it: a page that fails to load for a transient reason (a network blip, a slow server, a bad CDN response) is indistinguishable, from the pushed file's own contents, from a page genuinely removed from the site. Both are simply absent. The original policy swept both alike.

That concern was correct. It's checked directly against the crawl-time and push-time code, not just against what the client said: a page that times out mid-crawl produces the same kind of entry — a dropped-log row, nothing in the pushed file — as a page that returns a clean 404. Nothing downstream could tell them apart, so nothing downstream should have deleted on either signal alone.

02

The conflict Weikai's "just don't delete" request runs into

Weikai's own counter-proposal was a persistent inventory — URL, response status, content checksum — diffed crawl over crawl, so a page only comes out of the index on a confirmed 404, never on a fetch failure. Building that is real, scoped work: new persistent state, a new comparison step, a new thing to keep correct across every site. That's the conflict this document originally closed as unreconcilable with the contract as scoped.

What that framing missed: the crawler already classifies why a URL failed, per request, before this conversation ever started. ArchiveSpiderMixin._log_http_error writes one of http_404, http_5xx, http_3xx, or network_error:<type> to *_dropped.csv — today, on every crawl, for every site. Nothing needed inventing. The fix is narrower than the conflict this section originally posed: read the one reason that already means "confirmed gone," carry it across the S3 boundary as an explicit marker instead of leaving deletion to be inferred from absence, and leave every other reason alone. No checksums, no new persistent store — the conflict was solvable inside contracted scope because the signal was already being computed and thrown away.

03

Every scenario, in one table

Ten of these thirteen rows are the crawl-time circuit breaker and push-time abort checks (ABORT_CONDITIONS.md) — untouched by this change, since they all run before reconciliation ever sees a file. Three rows change outcome. Two more, not in Weikai's original complaint at all, surface a deliberate policy this design commits to: never delete on an ambiguous signal, only on a confirmed one. See 06 for how that policy gets audited rather than left to accumulate silently.

ScenarioDropped-log reasonOutcome nowStatus
Page genuinely removed http_404 Explicit tombstone row → targeted delete of that URL's document, independent of timestamps. Removed — correct
Isolated timeout or 5xx, below ERROR_THRESHOLD network_error:* / http_5xx Not tombstoned, absent from the file either way — left untouched. Previously swept and deleted this run. Fixed by this change
Content-page timeouts reach CONTENT_PAGE_TIMEOUT_THRESHOLD (5) in one crawl critical_timeout_threshold Spider closes outright; push aborts unconditionally. Nothing reaches reconciliation this cycle. Unchanged
5xx/network rows reach ERROR_THRESHOLD at push time count ≥ threshold Push aborts entirely; --bypass required to override. Nothing pushed, nothing reconciled. Unchanged
Empty-200 (CDN defect) on an ordinary content page network_error:EmptyResponseError Not tombstoned — the reason isn't http_404 — so it's left untouched instead of recurring indefinitely on every affected run. Also fixed (unintended win)
Empty-200 on a listing-pagination or sitemap request critical_pagination: / critical_sitemap: Unconditional abort on the first occurrence, before reconciliation is reached. Unchanged
Lost sitemap or sub-sitemap fetch critical_sitemap:* Unconditional abort, no count, no --bypass. Unchanged
Listing-pagination or sitemap timeout, even once critical_pagination:* Spider closes immediately; push aborts unconditionally. Unchanged
*_dropped.csv missing entirely n/a — crash signal Hard abort, no --bypass. Unchanged
Main CSV has zero rows n/a Hard abort, no --bypass. Unchanged
Page loses its last inbound link (4 link-crawled sites) no row anywhere — never requested No dropped-log entry exists to tombstone. Left in the index, deliberately - confirmed as the preferred default over auto-deleting on an ambiguous signal. See 06. Intentional — audit via last_seen_at
Page dropped by the site's own no_body/no_title filter rule excluded pre-conversion — no dropped-log entry Same as above — nothing to tombstone, left in place by the same policy. Intentional — audit via last_seen_at
Empty-200 on ordinary content page — duplicate of row 5, flagged separately in the original network_error:EmptyResponseError See row 5. No longer a distinct open case. Folded into row 5
04

The About Us case, worked through

openobamawhitehouse.archives.gov/about — evergreen, high-value, one of the pages most likely to be linked to from outside the archive. It last indexed clean on Sep 15. On the Sep 22 recrawl, a mid-run connection reset takes it out after both retries exhaust.

/about network_error:TCPTimedOutError
Sep 15
Indexed normally. last_seen_at = 2026-09-15.
Sep 22
Fetch fails, retries exhaust, logged to *_dropped.csv as network_error:TCPTimedOutError. Below ERROR_THRESHOLD — this one page's loss doesn't abort the push. The URL is absent from the pushed file either way.
Reconciled
Before this fork Absence from the file swept the document. /about drops out of search until the next clean crawl happens to succeed.
Now No http_404, no tombstone row. The document keeps its 2026-09-15 content, visibly a week stale, but present.
05

The decision tree

What changed structurally: the trigger for deletion moved from "is this URL missing from the file" to "does this URL carry an explicit gone-marker" — a one-branch difference with a very different failure mode on the wrong side of it.

06

What is closed, what is intended, and what is left for audit

Closed by this fork

  • A transient fetch failure no longer deletes a live page — the core of Weikai's complaint.
  • The empty-200/CDN-defect case no longer recurs indefinitely — flagged as open in the original, resolved as a side effect.
  • Deletion no longer depends on last_seen_at comparisons at all — it's carried explicitly, row by row.

Intended, unchanged

  • Every crawl-time and push-time abort check (rows 3, 4, 6–10) — none of them touch reconciliation logic.
  • --bypass still only ever skips the ordinary-failure threshold, never the critical or crash checks.
  • A real 404 still removes a page, now more directly than before.

Left for audit, not auto-deleted

  • A page that loses its last inbound link, or gets filtered by a content-quality rule, is left in the index rather than removed — confirmed as the preferred default: keep stale content, review before removing it.
  • Real exposure, not hypothetical: the 4 link-crawled sites (open.obamawhitehouse, www.obamawhitehouse, letsmove.obamawhitehouse, www.trumpwhitehouse) track source sites that receive real quarterly updates, under a weekly crawl cadence meant to catch exactly that kind of change.
  • last_seen_at is the audit signal — already stamped on every document, already read by the Lambda's own freshness gate. No new field, no new pipeline.

Every document not reconfirmed by a source_site's most recent crawl keeps its old last_seen_at while its siblings move forward — that gap is the whole audit mechanism. One query, scoped to a site, surfaces every candidate oldest-first: 

GET archive_content_v2/_search
{
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "must": [
        { "term": { "source_site.keyword": "open.obamawhitehouse" } },
        { "range": { "last_seen_at": { "lt": "<most-recent-crawl's-last_seen_at-for-this-site>" } } }
      ]
    }
  },
  "sort": [{ "last_seen_at": "asc" }]
}

This is close to a mirror of _max_indexed_last_seen_at, the aggregation lambda_function.py's own freshness gate already runs on every push — that function asks "what's the newest last_seen_at for this site," this asks the inverse, "what's fallen behind it." No new capability, just pointed the other direction.
